column2: Splitting through the palate of the great-souled brahmana, a great blaze of light went up then to heaven.
Then a great cry of "Alas!" arose in all quarters; that light, praised, entered Brahma then.
Then the Grandfather, going forth to meet that light as a person a span in size, said "Welcome," lord of the people.
And he spoke again sweet words: "The fruit of yogas is equal to that of the mutterers; there is no doubt.
Of these, the fruit of yoga is seen directly; but for mutterers the rising to meet is special and greater.
Dwell in me, if you are joined." Thinking so, the brahmana, free of fever, then entered his mouth.
The king too, by this method, entered the blessed Grandfather, just as the tiger among the twice-born had.
Then the gods, saluting the Self-born, said: "This effort is for the sake of mutterers; for that we have come.
These two, honoured, are of equal fruit with you; the great fruit of yoga and of muttering is seen today; passing all worlds, these two may go where they wish."
[Brahma said:] "He who reads the Mahasmriti and likewise the auspicious Anusmriti, these two also by this method may go to my world.
And whoever is devoted to yoga, he too, without doubt, by this method, at the end of his body, will gain my worlds. Go; I shall accomplish each place for success."
[Bhishma said:] Having spoken so, the god then vanished there; the gods, taking leave of him, went each to his dwelling.
And all those great souls, having honoured Dharma there, followed behind, king, all with well-pleased minds.
This is the fruit of the mutterers, and their goal has been told as heard; what more do you wish to hear, great king?"
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Manu, lord of creatures, and the great sage Brihaspati.
Brihaspati, great sage, chief of the hosts of gods and sages, as a disciple bowing to his teacher, asked this old question of Prajapati, the best on earth:

For what reason has the rule of mantras come about, and what do the brahmins call the fruit in knowledge? That which is not revealed by the words of mantras: tell me that, blessed one, as it is.
mahabharata:12:194.5	What is it that the knowers of the scriptures of wealth and of mantras seek with many sacrifices and gifts of choice cows, as great fruit? What is it, how and where will it be?
mahabharata:12:194.6	The earth, the plants, the wind, the sky, the water-dwellers and the water, heaven and the dwellers in heaven: from what are they born? Tell me that ancient matter, blessed one.
mahabharata:12:194.7	From what a man seeks knowledge, for that the activity is aimed; and I do not know the ancient supreme; how then should I make false activity?
mahabharata:12:194.8	Having studied the Rig, Sama and Yajus collections, the metres, the course of the stars, etymology, grammar, ritual and phonetics, I do not know the nature of beings.
mahabharata:12:194.9	Let you tell me all this: the fruit in knowledge or in action, how the embodied one leaves the body, and how he enters a body again.

[Manu said:] "Whatever is dear to someone they call happiness; that same, unwished for, they call sorrow. 'Let the wished be mine and the other not': for this the rule of action arose. 'Let neither the wished nor the unwished touch me': for this the rule of knowledge arose.

The works in the Veda are of desire; freed from these, one would reach the supreme. A man on the manifold path of action, seeking happiness, does not reach the supreme; for that supreme is apart from the path of action, without hope, and is surely Brahman.
Beings were created by mind and by action; both these are good paths, honoured by the world. Seeing that action is eternal and also has an end, giving up the mind is the cause and nothing else.
Like an eye leading by its own self, with the self covered in darkness at night's end, knowledge joined with the quality of discernment sees the inauspicious deed, to be avoided.
Men avoid snakes, sharp points of grass and a well, knowing them; the foolish fall into them through ignorance; see how in knowledge the fruit is special.
The whole mantra properly used, sacrifices as prescribed with fees, gift of food, and concentration of mind: they say the fruit of action is fivefold.

The Vedas say action is of the nature of the qualities; therefore the mantras, for action has mantras as its root; the rule is to be done, accomplished by the mind, the embodied one being the enjoyer of the fruit.

Sounds, forms, tastes that are good, touches and scents that are auspicious: a man reaching the state of embodiment could be lord of these; this is the fruit that is accomplished by action in the world.
Whatever action one does by the body, joined to the body he gains the fruit of that; the body is the seat of happiness, and the body is also the seat of sorrow.
What action one does by speech, by speech alone he gains all of that; and what action one does by the mind, abiding in the mind he gains that.
As the seeker of fruit does a host of acts by their quality, intent on the fruit of action, so, joined with the qualities, he enjoys the good and bad fruit of action.
As a fish going against the current, so a deed done before comes to the doer; let the embodied one be pleased with good, but he is not pleased with evil deeds.
That from which all this world was born, which self-possessed ones know and cross beyond, and which is not revealed by the words of mantras: hear from me, as it is told, that supreme.
Free of tastes and of various scents, soundless, touchless, formless, ungraspable, unmanifest, colourless, one, it created the fivefold kind of beings.
Neither woman, man nor neuter, neither being nor non-being, nor being and non-being, which the knowers of Brahman among men do not see: know that to be the imperishable, which does not decay."
[Brihaspati said:] "These, going to water with their bodies, and from water to fire, wind and sky, return from space those who are not to be; those who are to be reach the supreme.
Not hot, not cold, not soft, nor sharp, not sour, astringent, sweet or bitter; not with sound nor with scent, nor with form: that is the supreme nature.
The body knows touch, the tongue taste, the nose smells, the ear sounds, the eye forms; but they do not grasp the supreme, those men who do not know the self.
Having turned the tongue from tastes, the nose from smells, the ear from sound, the body from touch and the eye from the quality of form, then he sees the supreme, his own nature.
That by which one takes up and does, that in which one begins activity, that in which and by which and whoever is the doer: they call it the cause, the means.

That which is lord, accomplishing and pervading, which is praised in the world as having mantras, which is the cause of all and accomplishes the supreme aim: that is the cause; other than that is effect.
As a man gains good and bad by his own good deeds without obstruction, so in good and bad bodies this knowledge is bound by deeds born of oneself.
As a lamp lit in front gives light to another as it burns, so here the five-sensed lamp-trees, lit by knowledge, stand out.
As, churning those same logs, one sees smoke and flame by combination, so the wise man, by the sameness of the senses, sees the supreme, his own nature.
As one sees in a dream one's own limb fallen on the earth, as another's, so the one joined to hearing and the rest, with good mind and good understanding, goes from one subtle body to another.
He is not joined to birth, growth, decay and meeting, this supreme embodied one; by this subtle body he goes unseen to another subtle body by the joining of rebirth.
He does not see his own form with the eye, nor does he touch anything with the sense of touch, nor does he accomplish his task by them; they do not see him, he sees them.
As in a burning lamp's fire a form born of heat is found, yet it does not bear an inner quality of form, so his form is seen.
As a man leaves the body and enters another unseen, abandoning the body in the great elements, and bears a form dependent on them,
the embodied one enters space, wind, fire, water and earth on every side; hearing and the other four, relying on different supports, serve the qualities in action.
Hearing is from space, smell from earth, form is of fire, digestion too; sweat is said to rest on water, taste also, and the quality that makes touch belongs to wind.
In the great elements dwell the five, and the five objects of sense in the senses; all of these follow the mind; the mind follows intellect; mind has its own nature.
Whatever good or bad deed is done by him, he takes up in his own body; high and low follow the mind, as water-dwellers follow the current.
It moves as it comes into the path of sight; subtle, it descends as a great form; it observes its own form, and then comes to the path of the higher intellect."
[Manu said:] "As he does not see all the objects of the senses at once, in the same time, but moves by strength as he is able, learned one, therefore he is one, the supreme embodied one.
Rajas, tamas and, third, sattva: he goes to the diverse qualities of knowledge; the embodied one enters the senses as wind enters fire in fuel.
He does not see his own form with the eye, nor touch with the sense of touch; the mark of hearing is not seen in the ear; one who sees thus, that perishes.
Hearing and the rest do not see their own self by themselves; the omniscient, all-seeing knower of the field sees them.
As the side of the Himalaya and the back of the moon were not seen before by men, yet they are not for that reason nonexistent,
so the self of beings among beings, subtle and made of knowledge, was not seen before with eyes, yet is not for that reason nonexistent.
As though looking, one does not find the mark in the moon in the world, so whether this exists or not, that is not without a resort.
The wise see by thought the sun's rising and setting, which has form because it has no form; absorbed in it, they see the sun's course.
The snake alone sees the feet of the snake: such is the example; so the one in forms, resting in forms, is to be known and sees by knowledge.
As the senses are not able to know the senses, so here the supreme intellect does not see the supreme by intellect.
As the moon on the new-moon night is not seen because it has no mark, yet it is not destroyed, so know the embodied one.
The moon, its store spent, does not shine on the new moon; so the embodied one, parted from form, is not perceived.
As the moon, reaching another store, shines again, so the embodied one, reaching another subtle body, shines again.
His birth, growth and decay are seen directly, but that is the moon's manifestation, not that of the embodied one.
As it is taken as "the same" by origin, growth and loss, the moon alone on the new moon is thus embodied.
Darkness is seen neither approaching nor leaving the moon; see the embodied one likewise as leaving and approaching.
As darkness is found joined with moon and sun, so the embodied one is found joined with the body.
As Rahu, freed from moon and sun, is not found, so the embodied one, freed from the body, is not found.
As the moon on the new moon goes and is joined with the stars, so the embodied one, freed from the body, is joined with the fruits of action.
As in clear water one sees a form with the eye, so one with clear senses sees the knowable by knowledge.
As in that same water when stirred one does not see the form, so when the senses are agitated one does not see the knowable by knowledge.
Lack of understanding is made by ignorance; the mind is spoiled by lack of understanding; of the spoiled mind, five mental faults arise.
One satisfied with ignorance, plunged in objects, is not seen; but the pure-souled, without seeing, turns back from objects.
The cutting of craving does not happen in a man through his impurity; craving turns back as sin comes to its end.
By contact with objects and through lack of resort to the eternal, desiring another with the mind, he does not reach the supreme.
Knowledge arises in men by the destruction of sinful action; then he sees the self in the self, as in the surface of a mirror.
With the senses let loose, one is in sorrow; with them restrained, in happiness; therefore one should restrain the self by the self from the forms of the senses.
He who gives up sounds and the rest, and all manifestations, releases the host of forms; leaving them, he enjoys immortality.
As the sun at its rising sends out the circle of its rays, and at its setting draws them back into itself,
so the inner self, entering the body with the rays of the senses and gaining the five qualities of the senses, covers them and goes to its setting.
Led again and again along the path laid down by action, this self-possessed one gains the grown fruit of action and dharma.
Objects turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food; even the taste turns back, seeing the supreme.
When intellect, free of the qualities of action, abides in the mind, then Brahman is attained and dissolved right there.
Untouching, unhearing, untasting, unseeing, unsmelling, unreasoning, he enters the supreme sattva.
Forms are sunk in the mind; the mind has passed beyond to intellect; intellect has passed beyond to knowledge; knowledge has reached the supreme.
The success of the mind is by the senses; the mind does not know intellect; intellect does not know the unmanifest; the subtle one sees these."
[Manu said:] "When intellect, joined with the qualities of action, abides in the mind, then Brahman is known by meditation, yoga and concentration.
This intellect with qualities turns upon the qualities themselves, like water flowing down from a mountain peak.
When he reaches qualityless meditation, which comes before in the mind, then Brahman is known, as a touchstone on a touchstone.
The mind, carried off by intellect, shows the objects of the senses; the example of the qualityless is not before the eye, which sees qualities.
Having closed all these doors and abiding in the mind, making the mind one-pointed, he reaches that supreme.
As the great elements turn back at the destruction of the qualities, so intellect, taking up the senses, abides in the mind.
When that intellect abides in the mind, moving within, endowed with the quality of resolve, then it becomes mind.
When the mind, endowed with qualities, has the quality of meditation, then, giving up all qualities, he reaches the qualityless.
In the knowledge of the unmanifest there is no equal example; where there is no footstep, who could reach that object?
By austerity, inference, qualities, birth and learning, one should lead to that supreme Brahman with a purified inner self.
The one without qualities follows that path outwardly; because of the absence of qualities, and by nature, it is beyond reasoning, measured by the knowable.
From being without qualities one reaches Brahman; from having qualities one turns back; intellect spreads over qualities like fire in fuel.
As the five senses are freed from their own actions, so the supreme Brahman is freed, beyond nature.
Thus all embodied beings arise from nature; they return, and at the return they do not go to anything.
The Person, nature, intellect, the specific forms and the senses, ego and conceit arise, called the elements.
The first activity of one proceeds from the primal; the second, the pairing, brings the manifest without distinction.
From dharma the good is lifted up, and likewise the not-good from adharma; the attached goes to nature, the detached becomes a knower."
[Manu said:] "And as the thread runs again through gold, through pearls, coral, clay and silver,
so, attached by his own deeds, the soul is in cows, in men, in elephants, deer and the rest, in insects and moths.
By whatever body he does whatever deed, by that same body he enjoys the fruit of that.
As the earth, of one taste, follows the nature of herbs, so intellect follows action and sees the inner self.
Desire arises preceded by knowledge, and intent follows desire; action is preceded by intent; action is the root, then the fruit.
Know the fruit to be of the nature of action, action of the nature of the knowable, the knowable of the nature of knowledge, and knowledge of the nature of being and non-being.
At the end of knowledges, fruits, knowables and actions, the fruit is divine knowledge, established in the knowable.
The great supreme being is seen by yogis who are joined; the unawake, who rest in themselves and take the qualities as intellect, do not see it.
Because it is without beginning, middle or end, it is imperishable; it passes beyond all sorrows, for sorrow is said to have an end.
That is called the supreme Brahman, that is held to be the supreme abode; going to it, freed from the domain of time, they rest in liberation.
These shine through the qualities; beyond them, because of being without qualities, the dharma marked by withdrawal leads to the endless.
The Rik, Yajus and Saman verses rest on the body and move on the tips of tongues; accomplished by effort, they are perishable.
Brahman is not held to arise from the support of the body; it is not accomplished by effort; it has no beginning, middle or end.
The beginning of the Riks and of the Samans and of the Yajus is spoken of; the end of those with beginnings is seen; but Brahman is not held to have a beginning.
Because it has no beginning and no end, it is endless and imperishable; because imperishable it is beyond the pairs; because of the absence of pairs, it is supreme.
Because it is unseen, without means, and without connection to action, mortals do not see it by that by which they go to the supreme.
By contact with objects, and by seeing the eternal, desiring another with the mind, he does not reach the supreme.
Those who see qualities here desire them; others do not seek the supreme, as seekers of qualities, because it is without qualities.
How can one joined with the lower qualities know these qualities? By inference, along with the qualities and their parts, one is to go.
We know it by the subtle mind; we cannot express it by speech; for the mind is to be grasped by the mind, and sight by sight.
Having cleansed the intellect by knowledge, and the mind by intellect, and the host of senses by mind, he reaches the endless.
Without intellect, unprosperous in mind, and so hopeless, he reaches quality; those who are tempted give up the supreme, like wind in fire set in fuel.
In taking up and in separating from the qualities, the mind, with higher and lower intellect, being engaged by this very rule, in taking up the qualities reaches Brahman's body.
The Person, with unmanifest self and unmanifest action, goes to unmanifestness at the end of time; by those same senses, growing or fading, he lives in the form of action.
The body, joined with all the senses and resting on the five elements, is obtained; it does not go by action here for lack of power; and deprived of that, it is deprived of the supreme imperishable.
A man does not see the end of the earth, and know that it will have an end; they lead the tempted to the supreme, as the wind a raft on the sea.
As the sun, seeing quality, becomes qualityless when his circle of rays has gone, so this sage here, free of distinction, enters qualityless, imperishable Brahman.
The goal of the virtuous from which there is no return, the self-born, the origin and store, eternal, the immortal imperishable seat: pondering it, he gains peace and immortality."
[Yudhishthira said:] "I wish to hear in truth, best of the Bharatas, about Narayana, Hrishikesha, Govinda, the unconquered Keshava."
[Bhishma said:] "This matter has been heard from Rama Jamadagnya as he spoke, from Narada the divine sage, and from Krishna Dvaipayana.
Asita Devala, dear, and Valmiki of great austerity, and Markandeya tell the great wonder in Govinda.
Keshava, best of the Bharatas, the blessed lord, master, is heard of as the Person, as all, in many ways, the pervader.
But hear, Yudhishthira, mighty-armed, the glories of the bearer of the Sharnga bow which the brahmanas know in the world.
And what the knowers of the Puranas say, lord of men, I shall tell in full about Govinda.
The great-souled best of Persons, the self of beings, arranged the great elements: wind, fire, water, space and earth.
Having seen the earth, that lord of all beings, the great-souled best of Persons, made his sleep on the waters.
There the blessed god, lighting the quarters in the lotus, became Brahma, dear, the grandfather of all beings.
When that great soul appeared, the great asura named Madhu was born, older than darkness.
Fierce, of fierce deeds, devoted to fierce thoughts, him the best of Persons slew, doing honour to Brahma.
From his slaying, dear, all gods, Danavas and men call him Madhusudana, the bull of all the Satvatas.
Brahma created mental sons, with Daksha as seventh: Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha and Kratu.
Marichi created Kashyapa, dear, his eldest son; he brought forth the mental, radiant best of Brahmanas.
Brahma created from his thumb one who was born even before Marichi; he, best of the Bharatas, became the lord of creatures called Daksha.
Ten and three daughters were born to him earlier, Bharata, daughters of that lord of creatures; the eldest of them was Diti.
Marichi's son Kashyapa, knower of all special dharmas, of holy fame and great renown, became the husband of them all.
Having begotten them, the great Daksha, lord of creatures and knower of dharma, gave ten of the younger ones to Dharma.
Dharma's sons were the Vasus and the Rudras of immeasurable splendour, the Vishvedevas, Sadhyas and Marutvants, Bharata.
Of the younger ones, twenty-seven others; Soma, greatly fortunate, became the husband of all of them.
The others bore gandharvas, horses, birds, cows, kimpurushas, fish and sprout-born plants.
Aditi bore the Adityas, the best of gods, of great strength; among them Vishnu was Vamana, and the lord Govinda.
By his stride the fortune of the gods grew, and the Danavas were overcome, with the Daitya and asura subjects.
Danu created the Danavas with Viprachitti foremost; Diti bore all the asuras of great strength.
Madhusudana arranged day and night, time, the seasons, forenoon and afternoon, all of it.
By thought he made the waters, clouds, and the moving and unmoving; he made the whole earth, with great splendour.
Then, Yudhishthira, mighty-armed Krishna again created from his mouth a hundred best brahmanas.
From his arms a hundred kshatriyas, from his thighs a hundred vaishyas, and from his feet a hundred shudras, Keshava, bull of the Bharatas.
Having thus created the four classes, the lord of great fame made a supervisor over all beings, the Creator.
As long as men had faith to sustain the body, so long they lived; there was no fear made by Yama.
Nor was there the dharma of union for them, best of the Bharatas; offspring arose for them by intention alone.
In the Treta age offspring were born by intention; there was no dharma of union for them even then, lord of men.
In the Dvapara the dharma of union arose among the people, king, and in the Kali age, king, people fell into pairs.
This is the lord of beings and his own overseer, dear, as told; but those without an overseer, Kaunteya, I shall tell also.
Those born in the southern region are all Talavaras, Andhrikas, Utsas, Pulindas, Shabaras, Chuchupas and Mandapas.
I shall tell also of those born in the northern region: Yaunas, Kambojas, Gandharas, Kiratas with Barbaras.
These, dear, doers of sin, roam this earth, lord of men, like dogs, crows and vultures in their ways.
These did not roam this earth in the Krita age, dear; from the Treta on, those people exist, best of the Bharatas.
Then, in that very terrible twilight at the end of the age, kings clashed, approaching one another.
Thus, best of the Kurus, this appearance of the great soul was told by Narada, the divine sage who sees all the worlds.
Narada, too, king, considered Krishna's eternity supreme, mighty-armed, best of the Bharatas, as it is.
So this mighty-armed Keshava, of true valour, lotus-eyed, inconceivable, is not merely a man."
[Bhishma said:] "Hear, best of the Bharatas, what you ask me: the lords of creatures who are each remembered in the directions.
There is one Self-born, the blessed primal eternal Brahma; Brahma had seven great-souled self-born sons.
Marichi, Atri, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu and the greatly fortunate Vasishtha, equal to the Self-born.
These are the seven Brahmas, as settled in the Purana; beyond this I shall tell of all the Prajapatis.
Born in the line of Atri, of Brahma's womb, eternal, was the blessed Prachinabarhis; from him came the ten Prachetases.
The one son of the ten was the Prajapati named Daksha; he has two names in the world, Daksha and Ka.
Kashyapa, son of Marichi, has two names heard of: one is Arishtanemi and the other they know as Kashyapa.
And Anga, his own son, the glorious king, and Bhauma, the mighty, who attended a thousand divine ages.
Pusha, Tvashta, Indra, and Vishnu, said to be the twelfth: these are the twelve Adityas, born of Kashyapa himself.
Nasatya and Dasra are remembered as the two Ashvins, sons of Martanda, the eighth of the Prajapati's sons.
And Tvashta's son was the glorious Vishvarupa of great fame; Ajaikapad, Ahirbudhnya, Virupaksha, Raivata,
Hara, Bahurupa, Tryambaka, lord of the gods, Savitra, Jayanta, and the unconquered Pinakin: the eight Vasus, greatly fortunate, were named earlier.
Such gods as these are of Manu the Prajapati; they and the earlier gods are remembered as the two kinds of ancestors.
Others delight in character and form, and others among the Siddhas and Sadhyas; the Ribhus and Maruts are the urged hosts of the gods.
So these are recorded: the Vishvedevas and the Ashvins; the Adityas are their kshatriyas, and the Maruts their vaishyas.
The Ashvins are held to be shudras, absorbed in fierce austerity; the Angiras gods are remembered as brahmanas, so it is settled. Thus the fourfold order of all the gods is told.
He who rises at dawn and recites these gods is freed from all sin, whether born of himself or done by another.
Yavakrita, Raibhya, Arvavasu, Paravasu, Aushija, Kakshivan and Nala were sons of Angiras.
Kanva, son of the sage Medhatithi, and Barhishada, dear, who are makers of the three worlds, are the seven sages of the east.
Unmucha, Vimucha, Svastyatreya the mighty, Pramucha, Idhmavaha and the blessed Dridhavrata,
and Agastya, the mighty son of Mitra and Varuna: these Brahmarshis ever rest in the southern quarter."
In his realm there was no wretched man, nor any in misery, nor sick, nor emaciated; no man anywhere was so.
Those two, rivals too, king, lived apart from each other; and Brihaspati troubled Samvarta again and again.
I know that the kingdom and yourself are afflicted, and by these words, lord of men, I know you are grieved.
Whatever grass they tore up and threw, king, appeared then as a firm club, like a thunderbolt.
The perfected ones went in their own aerial cars, moving as they wished, all stainless and holy, pure in speech, thought and deed.
There are two heaps, of good and of bad, bull among men; he who enjoys good first goes to hell afterward; he who is destined for hell first goes to heaven afterward.
